vignette:
He is a 41-year-old South Asian man who works as a graphic designer and lives with his wife in a small apartment near the city center. Before the traumatic event, he describes himself as careful, organized, and quietly proud of the life he and his wife had built together. His work has always been a place where he can lose himself in color, layout, and detail. He says he likes deadlines better than people because deadlines are predictable. That sense of control begins to change after an encounter with police that leaves him frightened, humiliated, and unable to shake the feeling that he is still in danger.

The incident happens on an evening when he is driving home after staying late at the office to finish a branding project. He is tired and distracted, thinking about whether he has locked the studio door and whether his wife has eaten dinner yet. When police stop him, the situation escalates quickly. He remembers the flashing lights first, then the sharpness in the officers' voices, then the feeling that he cannot explain himself well enough to make the moment end. He says that what frightens him most is not only the force of the encounter, but how small and exposed he feels in it. He is detained long enough for his body to go cold and his mind to keep repeating the same thought: if he says the wrong thing, this gets worse. Even after he is released, he feels shaken and ashamed, as though he has done something wrong simply by being there.

In the days afterward, he tries to return to work, but concentration slips away from him. He opens design files and stares at them without absorbing what he sees. Colors that usually feel energizing now seem harsh. The buzzing of his phone makes his chest tighten. He finds himself checking the locks on the apartment door more than once before bed, and he begins scanning the street when he leaves the building, noticing uniforms immediately. He does not talk much about the event at first. In his mind, he keeps revisiting different versions of what he might have said or done to avoid it. He feels embarrassed by how frightened he was and annoyed with himself for not remaining calm. He tells his wife that he is simply tired, but she notices that he sleeps lightly and wakes at small sounds.

As time passes, the memory of the encounter intrudes in fragments. He is sitting at his desk one afternoon adjusting font spacing when he suddenly feels the same rush of heat and helplessness he felt in the car. He has to step into the bathroom and grip the sink until the wave passes. He starts avoiding routes that pass police cars or stations, even if they are more efficient. If he hears sirens, his body reacts before his mind catches up: shoulders tightening, stomach dropping, heart racing. At night he has trouble settling. He lies awake replaying the incident in pieces, trying to remember details, then wishing he could erase them. On some nights he dreams he is being shouted at again and wakes before dawn with his heart pounding. Afterward he sits in the kitchen with tea he does not drink, listening to the apartment go quiet around him.

He becomes more guarded with other people, especially authority figures, and more easily irritated at home. When his wife asks what is wrong, he feels cornered and ashamed, then withdraws further. He notices that he is more on edge in public, more sensitive to tone of voice, more aware of hands moving near him. He avoids talking about the encounter because, in his mind, describing it makes it real again. Yet the silence also leaves him feeling alone and slightly unreal, as if he is living a life just beside his own.

Now, several sessions into therapy, he speaks more openly about how the event changed his sense of safety. He says he still functions outwardly, still completes projects, still jokes with coworkers when he must, but everything takes more effort. He no longer trusts his body in the same way; it seems to betray him with sudden surges of fear. He misses the version of himself who moved through the world without rehearsing explanations or measuring every interaction for danger. At home, he is trying to be patient with himself, though he finds that the smallest reminder-a siren, a uniform, a hard tone-can pull him back into the same knot of fear and humiliation he felt that night.
